lesson.title: The Generous Donor: Identifying the Reducing Agent
lesson.summary: A reducing agent is the species that causes another substance to be reduced by donating electrons to it, which means the reducing agent itself is oxidized.
lesson.body:
The reducing agent is the mirror image of the oxidizing agent, and it deserves the same careful, precise wording so the two never get swapped in your head: the reducing agent is the species that gets oxidized. It does the reducing to something else by handing over electrons, which means the reducing agent's own oxidation number goes up, not down, even though the word reducing sounds like it should describe something going down.

Go back to the zinc and copper example from earlier in this unit. Zinc metal went from oxidation number 0 to +2, losing 2 electrons, so zinc was oxidized. Because zinc is the species that got oxidized while causing Cu2+ to be reduced to copper metal, zinc is the reducing agent. Meanwhile Cu2+, the species that gained those 2 electrons and got reduced, is the oxidizing agent in that same reaction, exactly matching the definition from the last chapter.

Common reducing agents include active metals such as sodium, magnesium, zinc, and aluminum, which give up electrons readily, along with hydrogen gas, carbon, and ions like Fe2+ that can still lose another electron. Metallurgy leans on this heavily: a blast furnace extracts iron from iron ore using carbon monoxide as the reducing agent, Fe2O3(s) + 3CO(g) is right arrow 2Fe(s) + 3CO2(g). Check the atom balance: 2 iron atoms each side, and oxygen, 3 from Fe2O3 plus 3 from 3CO gives 6 on the left, matching 6 oxygen atoms across 3CO2 on the right. Balanced. Carbon monoxide is oxidized to carbon dioxide, carbon rising from +2 to +4, while iron is reduced from +3 to 0, which makes carbon monoxide the reducing agent and iron(III) oxide the oxidizing agent.

The fast identification trick mirrors the one for oxidizing agents: scan the reactant side, find the species whose oxidation number goes up over the course of the reaction, and that species is the reducing agent. Again, always look among the reactants, not the products, since the reducing agent is whatever a species was before it got oxidized, not what it turned into afterward.
